claim: The temporal envelope of speech is crucial for speech comprehension.
source: As the temporal envelope of speech is crucial for speech comprehension (Shannon et al., 1995), the ability to accurately encode temporal features in the auditory system is pivotal for successful perception of speech and conspecific vocalizations (Peelle and Wingfield, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shannon et al., 1995

claim: The ability to accurately encode temporal features in the auditory system is pivotal for successful perception of speech and conspecific vocalizations.
source: As the temporal envelope of speech is crucial for speech comprehension (Shannon et al., 1995), the ability to accurately encode temporal features in the auditory system is pivotal for successful perception of speech and conspecific vocalizations (Peelle and Wingfield, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peelle and Wingfield, 2016

claim: Age-related deficits have been observed in different temporal psychoacoustic tasks (e.g. gap detection).
source: Age-related deficits have been observed in different temporal psychoacoustic tasks (e.g. gap detection; Snell et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Snell et al., 2002

claim: The precision of processing of temporal cues declines with age.
source: Those psychoacoustic studies suggest that the precision of processing of temporal cues declines with age (e.g. Gordon-Salant et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon-Salant et al., 2006

claim: Age-related hearing loss has been attributed to a variety of peripheral declines in auditory coding.
source: While age-related hearing loss has been attributed to a variety of peripheral declines in auditory coding (e.g. Gates and Mills, 2005), fewer studies have looked at more central levels of auditory processing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gates and Mills, 2005

claim: Declines in temporal processing are hypothesized to be not exclusively peripheral in origin, but more central than at least the mid-brain.
source: Yet, declines in temporal processing are hypothesized to be not exclusively peripheral in origin, but more central than at least the mid-brain (Recanzone, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Recanzone, 2018

claim: In the aged macaque auditory cortex, neurons become more broadly tuned to temporal modulations.
source: In the aged macaque auditory cortex, neurons become more broadly tuned to temporal modulations and temporal fidelity of cortical responses decreases (Ng and Recanzone, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ng and Recanzone, 2018

claim: Temporal fidelity of cortical responses decreases in the aged macaque auditory cortex.
source: In the aged macaque auditory cortex, neurons become more broadly tuned to temporal modulations and temporal fidelity of cortical responses decreases (Ng and Recanzone, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ng and Recanzone, 2018

claim: In young macaques, A1 neurons have shorter response latencies than CL neurons.
source: In young macaques, the neuronal response to the inter-stimulus interval in primary field A1 and caudolateral belt area (CL) differs in that A1 neurons have shorter response latencies.
evidence: Inferred from the description of topographic neural dedifferentiation in the context of Ng and Recanzone, 2018

claim: In aged macaques, no difference in response latency was observed between A1 and CL neurons.
source: In aged animals, however, no difference was observed between A1 and CL such that aged A1 neurons had an equivalent response latency to CL neurons (Ng and Recanzone, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ng and Recanzone, 2018

claim: In aged neurons, a shift in neural coding strategy from less temporal coding towards more rate coding of temporal modulations was evident.
source: Further, in aged neurons, a shift in neural coding strategy from less temporal coding towards more rate coding of temporal modulations was evident (Overton and Recanzone, 2016; for a review of both coding strategies see Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Overton and Recanzone, 2016

claim: For neurons that still adhered to a temporal coding strategy, the temporal fidelity decreased in aged neurons.
source: For those neurons that still adhered to a temporal coding strategy, the temporal fidelity decreased, although the absolute number of neurons responsive to temporal modulations was unaffected by age (Overton and Recanzone, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Overton and Recanzone, 2016

claim: The absolute number of neurons responsive to temporal modulations was unaffected by age.
source: For those neurons that still adhered to a temporal coding strategy, the temporal fidelity decreased, although the absolute number of neurons responsive to temporal modulations was unaffected by age (Overton and Recanzone, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Overton and Recanzone, 2016

claim: The frontal and cingulo-opercular cortical response is elevated during a challenging speech comprehension or gap detection task in older listeners.
source: For example, the frontal and cingulo-opercular cortical response is elevated during a challenging speech comprehension or gap detection task (Erb and Obleser, 2013; Vaden et al., 2015; Vaden et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erb and Obleser, 2013; Vaden et al., 2015; Vaden et al., 2020

claim: Elevated frontal and cingulo-opercular cortical response has been interpreted as compensatory mechanism in response to loss of sensory acuity.
source: This has been interpreted as compensatory mechanism in response to loss of sensory acuity.
evidence: Inferred from the context of the preceding sentence about elevated cortical responses

claim: Aging has been hypothesized to lead to a neural dedifferentiation in sensory cortices.
source: Aging has been hypothesized to lead to a neural dedifferentiation in sensory cortices (e.g., Park et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2004

claim: With age, decoding accuracy of stimulus conditions from auditory cortical fMRI responses declines.
source: A more recent unspecific observation is that with age, decoding accuracy of stimulus conditions from auditory cortical fMRI responses declines (Lalwani et al., 2019; but see discussion for contrasting findings in MEG speech tracking, for example Presacco et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lalwani et al., 2019

claim: The decline in decoding accuracy has been linked to an imbalance of excitation and inhibition in older adults, more specifically a reduction of GABA levels in auditory cortex.
source: This finding in turn has been linked to an imbalance of excitation and inhibition in older adults, more specifically a reduction of GABA levels in auditory cortex (Lalwani et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lalwani et al., 2019

claim: Accumulating evidence supports the theory of an age-related loss of inhibition in sensory cortices.
source: Accumulating evidence supports the theory of an age-related loss of inhibition in sensory cortices (Caspary et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caspary et al., 2008

claim: Cortical processing of sounds is optimized to represent the spectro-temporal modulations which are typically present in conspecific vocalizations such as speech or animal calls.
source: A series of studies have shown that cortical processing of sounds is optimized to represent the spectro-temporal modulations which are typically present in conspecific vocalizations such as speech or animal calls (Santoro et al., 2014; Hullett et al., 2016; Santoro et al., 2017; Erb et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Santoro et al., 2014; Hullett et al., 2016; Santoro et al., 2017; Erb et al., 2019a

claim: The large-scale topographic organization of acoustic features is preserved in the older auditory cortex.
source: Results show that while the large-scale topographic organization of acoustic features is preserved in the older auditory cortex, age groups differ in tuning to temporal modulations: Human aging thus appears to be accompanied by an anatomically and functionally specific broadening of temporal-rate tuning in auditory cortex.
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: Age groups differ in tuning to temporal modulations.
source: Results show that while the large-scale topographic organization of acoustic features is preserved in the older auditory cortex, age groups differ in tuning to temporal modulations: Human aging thus appears to be accompanied by an anatomically and functionally specific broadening of temporal-rate tuning in auditory cortex.
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: Human aging is accompanied by an anatomically and functionally specific broadening of temporal-rate tuning in auditory cortex.
source: Results show that while the large-scale topographic organization of acoustic features is preserved in the older auditory cortex, age groups differ in tuning to temporal modulations: Human aging thus appears to be accompanied by an anatomically and functionally specific broadening of temporal-rate tuning in auditory cortex.
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: Sound identification accuracy was higher than chance level (0.5) for all models and age groups.
source: Sound identification accuracy was higher than chance level (0.5) for all models and age groups (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 2

claim: The sound mixture model had the highest sound identification accuracies.
source: The sound mixture model had the highest sound identification accuracies (Figure 2a) and thus described most accurately the fMRI responses to sounds.
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 2a

claim: Young participants had significantly higher identification accuracies for mixture than old participants.
source: Young participants had significantly higher identification accuracies for mixture than old participants (Figure 2a).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 2a

claim: There was no significant correlation between chronological age and sound identification accuracy for mixture within the young or older group.
source: There was no significant correlation between chronological age and sound identification accuracy for mixture within the young or older group (Figure 2b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 2b

claim: Tonotopic maps showed the typical mirror-symmetric frequency gradients along Heschl's gyrus in both young and aged auditory cortex, irrespective of age.
source: Tonotopic maps showed the typical mirror-symmetric frequency gradients along Heschl's gyrus in both young and aged auditory cortex, irrespective of age (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 3

claim: A low frequency region was observed in the central region of Heschl's gyrus (HG), presumably marking the boundary between the human homologue of primary auditory fields A1 and R.
source: Consistent with previous human fMRI data (Moerel et al., 2012), a low frequency region was observed in the central region of Heschl's gyrus (HG), presumably marking the boundary between the human homologue of primary auditory fields A1 and R (Figure 3a, red-yellow).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 3a, consistent with citation to Moerel et al., 2012

claim: The low frequency region was surrounded antero-medially and posteriorly by high frequency regions.
source: This low frequency region was surrounded antero-medially and posteriorly by high frequency regions (Figure 3a, green-blue).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 3a

claim: The antero-medial high frequency areas clustered on the planum polare (PP).
source: The antero-medial high frequency areas clustered on the planum polare (PP).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: The posterior regions preferring high frequencies covered planum temporale (PT).
source: The posterior regions preferring high frequencies covered planum temporale (PT).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: No significant age-group differences in tonotopic maps were found using two-sample voxel-wise t-tests (corrected for multiple comparisons).
source: We did not find significant age-group differences using two-sample voxel-wise t-tests (corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Based on the study's own statistical analysis

claim: Tonotopic group maps were correlated, indicating that topography for best frequency was preserved in older adults.
source: In fact, tonotopic group maps were correlated, indicating that topography for best frequency was preserved in older adults (Figure 3a).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 3a

claim: No significant voxel-wise age-group differences were found for best temporal and spectral modulation maps using two-sample t-tests (corrected for multiple comparisons).
source: Similarly, we did not find significant voxel-wise age-group differences using two-sample t-tests (corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Based on the study's own statistical analysis

claim: For both temporal and spectral modulations, group maps were correlated between age groups.
source: On the contrary, both for temporal and spectral modulations, group maps were correlated between age groups (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 4

claim: A medial-to-lateral gradient for increasing temporal rate was observed for best temporal modulation maps.
source: For best temporal modulation maps, we observed a medial-to-lateral gradient for increasing temporal rate (Figure 4a).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 4a

claim: For best spectral modulation maps, the locus of highest spectral resolution coincided with the low frequency region on Heschl's gyrus.
source: For best spectral modulation maps, the locus of highest spectral resolution coincided with the low frequency region on Heschl's gyrus (Figure 3a, Figure 4b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figures 3a and 4b

claim: Decoding yielded highest accuracies at frequencies of 230–580 Hz (mean r = 0.47) irrespective of age.
source: Decoding yielded highest accuracies at frequencies of 230–580 Hz (mean r = 0.47) and spectral scales of 0.25 cyc/oct (mean r = 0.47), irrespective of age (Figure 5a,b), indicating that brain responses followed the frequency and spectral modulation content of the stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 5a,b

claim: Decoding yielded highest accuracies at spectral scales of 0.25 cyc/oct (mean r = 0.47) irrespective of age.
source: Decoding yielded highest accuracies at frequencies of 230–580 Hz (mean r = 0.47) and spectral scales of 0.25 cyc/oct (mean r = 0.47), irrespective of age (Figure 5a,b), indicating that brain responses followed the frequency and spectral modulation content of the stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 5a,b

claim: For temporal modulations, reconstruction accuracies peaked at rates of 4–8 Hz (mean r = 0.4) in both age groups.
source: Conversely, for temporal modulations, reconstruction accuracies peaked at rates of 4–8 Hz (mean r = 0.4) in both age groups (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 5a,b

claim: The peaks in reconstruction accuracies at 4–8 Hz were not present in the stimuli.
source: Those peaks were not present in the stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a) and imply preferred processing of temporal rates in the speech-relevant range (Poeppel and Assaneo, 2020), corroborating our hypothesis (see also discussion).
evidence: Based on comparison with stimulus properties shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a

claim: The peaks in reconstruction accuracies at 4–8 Hz imply preferred processing of temporal rates in the speech-relevant range.
source: Those peaks were not present in the stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a) and imply preferred processing of temporal rates in the speech-relevant range (Poeppel and Assaneo, 2020), corroborating our hypothesis (see also discussion).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results and citation to Poeppel and Assaneo, 2020

claim: Selectivity of temporal rate coding was higher in young than in older participants (mean SI age difference = 0.01, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.68).
source: Selectivity of temporal rate coding was higher in young than in older participants (mean SI age difference = 0.01, p=0.004 [permutation test], Cohen's d = 0.68, Figure 5d, left).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 5d

claim: A lower selectivity index is consistent with a broadening of tuning in the aged auditory cortex.
source: A lower selectivity index is consistent with a broadening of tuning in the aged auditory cortex.
evidence: Inference from the selectivity index results

claim: The variance in the reconstruction accuracy profiles across the six temporal rate bins was higher in the young than in the older participants (mean difference in variance = 3.7×10−4, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.93).
source: Also, this key result of a broadened tuning to temporal rate was corroborated by an even simpler measure of selectivity: The variance in the reconstruction accuracy profiles across the six temporal rate bins (1–32 Hz, 'rate variance') was higher in the young than in the older participants (mean difference in variance = 3.7×10−4, p<0.001 [permutation test], Cohen's d = 0.93, Figure 6 a, left).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 6a

claim: In the older group, the rate variance was significantly correlated with the rate selectivity index.
source: In the older group, the rate variance was significantly correlated with the rate selectivity index and chronological age but was uncorrelated with hearing loss (Figure 6, b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 6b

claim: In the older group, the rate variance was significantly correlated with chronological age.
source: In the older group, the rate variance was significantly correlated with the rate selectivity index and chronological age but was uncorrelated with hearing loss (Figure 6, b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 6b

claim: In the older group, the rate variance was uncorrelated with hearing loss.
source: In the older group, the rate variance was significantly correlated with the rate selectivity index and chronological age but was uncorrelated with hearing loss (Figure 6, b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 6b

claim: The rate selectivity index in the older group was not significantly correlated with chronological age (Spearman's rho = −0.2, p=0.289).
source: Note however that the rate selectivity index (see above) in the older group was not significantly correlated with chronological age (Spearman's rho = −0.2, p=0.289), nor with hearing loss (Spearman's rho = 0.34, p=0.062).
evidence: Based on the study's own statistical analysis

claim: The rate selectivity index in the older group was not significantly correlated with hearing loss (Spearman's rho = 0.34, p=0.062).
source: Note however that the rate selectivity index (see above) in the older group was not significantly correlated with chronological age (Spearman's rho = −0.2, p=0.289), nor with hearing loss (Spearman's rho = 0.34, p=0.062).
evidence: Based on the study's own statistical analysis

claim: In a multiple regression predicting older participants' variance in rate from chronological age with covariates PTA and sound identification accuracy, age was significant (t(26) = −2.8, p=0.003).
source: In a multiple regression predicting older participants' variance in rate from chronological age with covariates PTA and sound identification accuracy, neither PTA (t(26) = 0.73, p=0.473, permutation test) nor sound identification accuracy (t(26) = 1.02, p=0.312) were significant, while age was significant (t(26) = −2.8, p=0.003; adjusted R2 = 0.39).
evidence: Based on the study's own statistical analysis

claim: In a multiple regression predicting older participants' variance in rate from chronological age with covariates PTA and sound identification accuracy, neither PTA nor sound identification accuracy were significant.
source: In a multiple regression predicting older participants' variance in rate from chronological age with covariates PTA and sound identification accuracy, neither PTA (t(26) = 0.73, p=0.473, permutation test) nor sound identification accuracy (t(26) = 1.02, p=0.312) were significant, while age was significant (t(26) = −2.8, p=0.003; adjusted R2 = 0.39).
evidence: Based on the study's own statistical analysis

claim: A decrease in the rate selectivity index with age was confirmed for HG/HS (mean SI difference = 0.012, p=0.009).
source: A decrease in the rate selectivity index with age was confirmed for HG/HS (mean SI difference = 0.012, p=0.009 [permutation test]) and PT (mean SI difference = 0.016, p=0.005 [permutation test]; see Figure 7b,c).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 7b,c

claim: A decrease in the rate selectivity index with age was confirmed for PT (mean SI difference = 0.016, p=0.005).
source: A decrease in the rate selectivity index with age was confirmed for HG/HS (mean SI difference = 0.012, p=0.009 [permutation test]) and PT (mean SI difference = 0.016, p=0.005 [permutation test]; see Figure 7b,c).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 7b,c

claim: The variance of the rate profiles was significantly higher in young than older adults in HG/HS (variance difference = 4×10−4, p=0.0004).
source: The alternative measure of selectivity, variance of the rate profiles, was also significantly higher in young than older adults in HG/HS (variance difference = 4×10−4, p=0.0004) and PT (variance difference = 5×10−4, p=0.0003).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: The variance of the rate profiles was significantly higher in young than older adults in PT (variance difference = 5×10−4, p=0.0003).
source: The alternative measure of selectivity, variance of the rate profiles, was also significantly higher in young than older adults in HG/HS (variance difference = 4×10−4, p=0.0004) and PT (variance difference = 5×10−4, p=0.0003).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: There were no age differences in temporal selectivity in PP, STG, STS or the control regions V1, SPG and MFG.
source: In contrast, there were no age differences in temporal selectivity in PP, STG, STS or the control regions V1, SPG and MFG (Figure 7d – i).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 7d-i

claim: Age-related changes in temporal selectivity selectively occur in primary auditory cortex and the planum temporale, but not surrounding belt areas.
source: These results indicate that age-related changes in temporal selectivity selectively occur in primary auditory cortex and the planum temporale, but not surrounding belt areas.
evidence: Inference from the ROI-specific results

claim: For spectral scale, a decreased SI in older adults was found in HG/HS (SI difference = 0.012, p=0.008).
source: For spectral scale, we also found a decreased SI in older adults in HG/HS (SI difference = 0.012, p=0.008) and PT (SI difference = 0.016, p=0.021), but none of the other ROIs (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: For spectral scale, a decreased SI in older adults was found in PT (SI difference = 0.016, p=0.021).
source: For spectral scale, we also found a decreased SI in older adults in HG/HS (SI difference = 0.012, p=0.008) and PT (SI difference = 0.016, p=0.021), but none of the other ROIs (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: For frequency, no age differences in selectivity index were found at all.
source: For frequency, we did not find any age differences in selectivity index at all (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: Topographic maps of acoustic feature preference for frequency, spectral and temporal modulations can be observed under approximately natural hearing situations.
source: Using natural stimuli, we revealed topographic maps of acoustic feature preference for frequency, spectral and temporal modulations. Thus, we show that topographic maps of feature preference can be observed under approximately natural hearing situations.
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: Tonotopic maps in younger versus older adults were highly correlated, indicating topographical stability of tonotopic organization across age groups.
source: Notably, tonotopic maps in younger versus older adults were highly correlated, indicating topographical stability of tonotopic organization across age groups.
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results

claim: In both young and older adults, a medial-to-lateral low-to-high gradient for temporal modulations was observed across the superior temporal plane.
source: Here, in both young and older adults we observed a medial-to-lateral low-to-high gradient for temporal modulations across the superior temporal plane (Figure 4a), while for spectral modulations, the locus with the highest resolution (~1.5 cyc/oct) was observed in lateral Heschl's gyrus (Figure 4b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 4a

claim: For spectral modulations, the locus with the highest resolution (~1.5 cyc/oct) was observed in lateral Heschl's gyrus.
source: Here, in both young and older adults we observed a medial-to-lateral low-to-high gradient for temporal modulations across the superior temporal plane (Figure 4a), while for spectral modulations, the locus with the highest resolution (~1.5 cyc/oct) was observed in lateral Heschl's gyrus (Figure 4b).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figure 4b

claim: A topographic representation for modulation rate has previously been observed in the primate auditory cortex.
source: A topographic representation for modulation rate has previously been observed in the primate auditory cortex (Baumann et al., 2015) where fast temporal acoustic information was preferably encoded in caudal auditory regions (Camalier et al., 2012; Kusmierek and Rauschecker, 2014) and slow temporal information in rostral areas R and RT (Liang et al., 2002; Bendor and Wang, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baumann et al., 2015; Camalier et al., 2012; Kusmierek and Rauschecker, 2014; Liang et al., 2002; Bendor and Wang, 2008

claim: Fast temporal acoustic information was preferably encoded in caudal auditory regions in primates.
source: A topographic representation for modulation rate has previously been observed in the primate auditory cortex (Baumann et al., 2015) where fast temporal acoustic information was preferably encoded in caudal auditory regions (Camalier et al., 2012; Kusmierek and Rauschecker, 2014) and slow temporal information in rostral areas R and RT (Liang et al., 2002; Bendor and Wang, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Camalier et al., 2012; Kusmierek and Rauschecker, 2014

claim: Slow temporal information was preferably encoded in rostral areas R and RT in primates.
source: A topographic representation for modulation rate has previously been observed in the primate auditory cortex (Baumann et al., 2015) where fast temporal acoustic information was preferably encoded in caudal auditory regions (Camalier et al., 2012; Kusmierek and Rauschecker, 2014) and slow temporal information in rostral areas R and RT (Liang et al., 2002; Bendor and Wang, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liang et al., 2002; Bendor and Wang, 2008

claim: Earlier human fMRI studies had failed to show a clear topography for modulation rate.
source: Whereas earlier human fMRI studies had failed to show a clear topography for modulation rate (Giraud et al., 2000; Schönwiesner and Zatorre, 2009; Overath et al., 2012; Leaver and Rauschecker, 2016), recent human fMRI (Santoro et al., 2014) and electrocorticography (ECoG) studies (Hullett et al., 2016) proposed the presence of a posterior-to-anterior high-to-low rate gradient in human auditory cortex.
evidence: Supported by citations to Giraud et al., 2000; Schönwiesner and Zatorre, 2009; Overath et al., 2012; Leaver and Rauschecker, 2016

claim: Recent human fMRI and ECoG studies proposed the presence of a posterior-to-anterior high-to-low rate gradient in human auditory cortex.
source: Whereas earlier human fMRI studies had failed to show a clear topography for modulation rate (Giraud et al., 2000; Schönwiesner and Zatorre, 2009; Overath et al., 2012; Leaver and Rauschecker, 2016), recent human fMRI (Santoro et al., 2014) and electrocorticography (ECoG) studies (Hullett et al., 2016) proposed the presence of a posterior-to-anterior high-to-low rate gradient in human auditory cortex.
evidence: Supported by citations to Santoro et al., 2014; Hullett et al., 2016

claim: Synthetic sounds lack both the behavioural relevance and the statistical structure of natural sounds.
source: As synthetic sounds lack both the behavioural relevance and the statistical structure of natural sounds, they activate auditory cortex differently than natural stimuli (Theunissen et al., 2000; Bitterman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Theunissen et al., 2000; Bitterman et al., 2008

claim: Synthetic sounds activate auditory cortex differently than natural stimuli.
source: As synthetic sounds lack both the behavioural relevance and the statistical structure of natural sounds, they activate auditory cortex differently than natural stimuli (Theunissen et al., 2000; Bitterman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Theunissen et al., 2000; Bitterman et al., 2008

claim: The observed decrease in selectivity reveals a broadening of temporal tuning functions with age under the assumption that the reconstruction accuracy reflects tuning properties of neuronal populations.
source: Under the assumption that the reconstruction accuracy reflects tuning properties of neuronal populations, the observed decrease in selectivity reveals a broadening of temporal tuning functions with age.
evidence: Inference from the study's results under a stated assumption

claim: The broadened temporal tuning may underlie the difficulties older adults experience in speech comprehension in noisy environments.
source: This finding provides mechanistic insights into the changes of temporal processing in the aging auditory cortex: The broadened temporal tuning, reminiscent of an age-related decrease in temporal precision in the midbrain (Anderson et al., 2012), may underlie the difficulties older adults experience in speech comprehension in noisy environments (Anderson et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2012 and Anderson et al., 2011

claim: Rate selectivity in the older listeners was statistically unrelated to their pure-tone audiograms.
source: While the present study lacks more direct measures of encoding along the auditory pathway, it is important to note that rate selectivity in the older listeners was statistically unrelated to their pure-tone audiograms (this holds true for both presented measures of tuning, the selectivity index [Figure 5] and the variance across temporal rates [Figure 6]).
evidence: Based on the study's own experimental results shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: The broadening of temporal tuning is not explicable merely by peripheral hearing loss.
source: Thus, the broadening of temporal tuning is not explicable merely by peripheral hearing loss.
evidence: Inference from the lack of correlation between rate selectivity and audiograms

claim: Evidence for better reconstruction of temporal envelopes from older listeners' MEG signals suggests an enhanced cortical envelope representation.
source: Evidence for better reconstruction of temporal envelopes from older listeners' MEG signals (Presacco et al., 2016) and larger N1 amplitudes in older adults with widened auditory filters (Herrmann et al., 2016; Henry et al., 2017) suggest an enhanced cortical envelope representation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Presacco et al., 2016; Herrmann et al., 2016; Henry et al., 2017

claim: Larger N1 amplitudes in older adults with widened auditory filters suggest an enhanced cortical envelope representation.
source: Evidence for better reconstruction of temporal envelopes from older listeners' MEG signals (Presacco et al., 2016) and larger N1 amplitudes in older adults with widened auditory filters (Herrmann et al., 2016; Henry et al., 2017) suggest an enhanced cortical envelope representation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Herrmann et al., 2016; Henry et al., 2017

claim: An inflated cortical representation of the speech envelope has been argued to be a maladaptive response as compensation of the lack of temporal precision in the midbrain.
source: However, an inflated cortical representation of the speech envelope has been argued to rather be a maladaptive response as compensation of the lack of temporal precision in the midbrain (Anderson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2012

claim: Fast temporal modulations (>50 Hz) are typically encoded through the rate code.
source: Fast temporal modulations (>50 Hz) are typically encoded through the rate code, while neurons tuned to slow temporal rates (<50 Hz) mostly synchronize to the sounds' modulations (temporal code, Sachs, 1984; Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sachs, 1984; Joris et al., 2004

claim: Neurons tuned to slow temporal rates (<50 Hz) mostly synchronize to the sounds' modulations (temporal code).
source: Fast temporal modulations (>50 Hz) are typically encoded through the rate code, while neurons tuned to slow temporal rates (<50 Hz) mostly synchronize to the sounds' modulations (temporal code, Sachs, 1984; Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sachs, 1984; Joris et al., 2004

claim: Evidence from electrophysiology suggests a change in coding strategy across neuronal populations in A1 from less temporal coding towards more rate coding of temporal modulations in aged animals.
source: Evidence from electrophysiology suggests a change in coding strategy across neuronal populations in A1 from less temporal coding towards more rate coding of temporal modulations in aged animals (Ng and Recanzone, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ng and Recanzone, 2018

claim: In young macaques, A1 neurons had higher vector strength than CL neurons in response to modulated signals.
source: In a direct comparison of the vector strengths (a metric of periodicity of the neuronal response to a modulated signal) as a function of the inter-stimulus interval, responses differed in young A1 and CL neurons such that A1 neurons had higher vector strength.
evidence: Inferred from the discussion of Ng and Recanzone, 2018 findings

claim: Inhibitory neurotransmitters have been shown to increase response synchrony to modulated stimuli in both the cochlear nucleus and the inferior colliculus.
